newsitem.title: SPAIN: Aznar asks Spain to rise above differences for EMU.
newsitem.headline: Aznar asks Spain to rise above differences for EMU.

text.p: Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar asked all political parties on Wednesday to make a united effort to get Spain into Europe's planned monetary union.

"All parliamentary groups have to work for the higher interest of Spain because we cannot, and we should not, waste one bit of the energy in Spanish society on minor squabbles," Aznar told Congress as he opened a state of the nation debate.
"We have to rise above our understandable individual uncertainty and justifiable impatience in the process of modernising Spain and gaining access to the monetary union."
Opposition leader Felipe Gonzalez replied that the Socialists were keen for a united front but the government was guilty of abusing its power.
Communist Julio Anguita, however, denounced the politics of consensus, saying the conservatives and the socialists were getting too cosy.
Aznar said 1998 and 1999 would be crucial years for Spain's future prosperity and called for political and social calm to complement the economic stability the country was enjoying.

"This government wants Spain to be among the first group of countries in the economic union, and wants to achieve this without undermining the levels of social protection that Spaniards feel they want," he said.

In the first state of the nation debate since Aznar's conservative government came to power last May, the prime minister happily rolled off a series of bright economic indicators: falling inflation, unemployment and deficit and better than expected growth.
He said Spain had met three of the five criteria for Europe's economic and monetary union and would not have "excessive difficulty" meeting the other two.
Opposition leader Felipe Gonzalez, who was prime minister for nearly 14 years, said his party fully backed efforts to join the EMU.
But he accused the government of stepping across ethical lines with its policies on TV soccer rights, health care, education and taxes.

"We are worried about some of the rules of the game," Gonzalez said. "There is not only an economic problem, there is also not only a problem of freedom of business, but there is also a political problem and it's called abuse of power."

The former prime minister, whose government was forced from power after a series of corruption scandals and accusations it waged a 1980s "dirty war" against Basque rebels, admitted mistakes had been made but said they should not be repeated.

Gonzalez said that although he had specific differences with Aznar, he was eager to put forward a united front not only on EMU, but also on the "fight against terrorism", the recently battered justice system, and foreign and regional policy.
Anguita, who leads parliament's third largest group, the United Left coalition, criticised the Socialists for swinging to the right and presenting a weak opposition.

"The serious thing is not the economic policy that the prime minister is undertaking, because he's doing what his politics and budget demand. The serious thing is the consensus that we find in this house," Anguita said.
The left-wing leader urged Aznar to pay more attention to human elements like the fight against hunger, unemployment, disease, and growing racial tensions, rather than a hard-nosed drive to EMU.
